questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Federalism: Meaning and Key Features' refers to.
questions.a: Federalism is a form of government in which sovereignty is constitutionally divided between a central authority and constituent units, each supreme in its own sphere. Its markers are two constitutionally guaranteed tiers of government, a written division of powers, and courts to arbitrate disputes between the tiers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Federalism: Meaning and Key Features'.
questions.a: Two governments, one constitution, no overlapping sovereignty -- federalism is power shared by design.

concepts.title: Federalism in the Indian Constitution: Union, States and Lists

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Federalism in the Indian Constitution: Union, States and Lists' refers to.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution creates a two-tier federation with a strong centre. The seventh schedule splits subjects into the union list, state list and concurrent list; residuary powers rest with the Union; and in emergencies the system bends toward unity, with Parliament empowered to legislate on state subjects.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Federalism in the Indian Constitution: Union, States and Lists'.
questions.a: A federation with a unitary tilt -- three lists, residuary power at the centre, and emergency levers that reshape the balance.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Federalism in the Indian Constitution: Union, States and Lists' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Conflict-Resolving Federalism: Language, Autonomy and Asymmetric Provisions

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Conflict-Resolving Federalism: Language, Autonomy and Asymmetric Provisions' refers to.
questions.a: Indian federalism has survived diversity by adjusting. The linguistic reorganisation of states in 1956 honoured language identities without breaking the union; special provisions under Articles 371 and former Article 370 accommodated particular histories; official bilingual policy and state autonomy demands show federation as continuous negotiation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Conflict-Resolving Federalism: Language, Autonomy and Asymmetric Provisions'.
questions.a: Flexibility over rigidity -- redrawing boundaries and granting accommodations kept the union together where rigidity would have split it.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Conflict-Resolving Federalism: Language, Autonomy and Asymmetric Provisions' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Centre-State Relations and Instruments of Central Control

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Centre-State Relations and Instruments of Central Control' refers to.
questions.a: Besides the lists, the centre holds levers that tilt the federation: governors appointed by the centre, the President's rule under Article 356, central grants and finance commission allocations, and all-India services staffing state administrations. Sarkaria and Punchhi commissions urged restraint in using these levers so cooperative federalism can work.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Centre-State Relations and Instruments of Central Control'.
questions.a: Governors, Article 356, grants and shared services -- the centre's levers, and the case for using them sparingly.
